## 8. Executable rigour — TOGAF, SAFe, PMP, MSP

The point of this section is that the rigour is **not a document library**. Every artefact below is a row with a
lifecycle; every gate is an approval; every claim links to evidence.

### 8.1 TOGAF ADM as an architecture capability

TOGAF's ADM is implemented as a **capability first and a project second**. The Preliminary phase establishes the
capability; an `architecture` project then walks the phases as WBS nodes; and every artefact a phase produces is a
typed row with a lifecycle, not a file in a library.

**The capability (Preliminary phase).** Six things are established before architecture work starts:

| Capability area | V2 row | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| Architecture principles | `architecture_artifact(type='principles_catalog')`; each entry `{uid, statement, rationale, implications}` | the Architecture Board approves the catalogue |
| Tailored ADM | `adm_profile(phase_set, artifact_requirements, contract_kinds)` — which phases, which artefacts are mandatory per phase and plateau, which contract closes each phase | the board adopts the profile |
| Repository and artefact standard | `artifact_type` catalogue (the standard's types, phase and plateau) + `architecture_artifact` rows | the repository is seeded and the standard adopted |
| Architecture Board | `governance_body(kind='architecture_board')` + membership, charter, commissioning authority and decision limits | the charter is approved and the board convened |
| Governance, contracts and waivers | `architecture_contract` + `architecture_waiver` | the governance baseline is recorded |
| Maturity and skills | `architecture_maturity(dimension, score 0–5, stage)` + `architecture_skill_assessment(role, skill, proficiency)` | the baseline is assessed and its development plan approved |

**The artefact standard.** `architecture_artifact` is the parent; **catalog**, **matrix** and **diagram** are its three
types, and each inherits the common metadata: title, status, version, author and date, reviewer and review date, the
related change initiative or project, the rationale (purpose, stakeholders, scope), and the published document or
the architecture contract it sits under. Type-specific metadata: a **catalog** names its unique identifier, item name
and description of use or structure; a **matrix** names its axes (usually two); a **diagram** names its building
block/metamodel and viewpoint. The entries are rows (`architecture_artifact_entry`: `axis_a`, `axis_b`, `value`), so a
catalogue is queryable and a matrix is joinable — an artefact is metadata plus entries plus a document, never a blob.

The standard groups artefacts into three **plateaus**: the **Project Start Architecture** (drivers/goals/objectives,
principles, stakeholders, requirements, actors/roles, application portfolio, solution concept, benefits), the
**High-Level Design** (business service/function, data entity/component, business interaction, application
organisation/data, business footprint, functional decomposition, conceptual data, technology standards), and the
**Solution Design** (process flows, logical data, interfaces, application communication/migration, technology
portfolio, platform decomposition, processing, project context). A project's tailored profile names which plateau its
current phase requires. Artefact-to-artefact dependencies are `architecture_artifact_link` edges
(`derivation | realization | reuse | dependency`), so the repository answers *what this artefact derives from, what it
realises, and what it reuses*.

**The phases.** Each phase is a WBS node; its mandatory artefact set comes from the standard, filtered by the
tenant's `adm_profile`; it closes on an approved `architecture_contract`; a phase cannot be skipped.

| Phase | Mandatory artefacts (from the standard) | Contract / gate |
|---|---|---|
| **Preliminary** | Principles Catalog; Principle Derivation and Principle Realization diagrams; tailored ADM profile; maturity and skills baseline | principles approved; capability adopted |
| **A — Vision** | Stakeholder Map and Matrix; Driver/Goal/Objective Catalog; Requirements Catalog; Solution Concept Diagram; **Statement of Architecture Work** | the SAW is approved (vision contract) |
| **B — Business** | Business Service/Function, Process/Event/Control/Product, Value Stream, Business Capabilities, Value Stream Stages, Contract/Measure catalogs; Business Interaction, Actor/Role, Value Stream/Capability, Strategy/Capability, Capability/Organization matrices; Business Footprint, Business Service/Information, Functional Decomposition, Product Lifecycle, Business Model Canvas, Business Capability Map, Value Stream Map, Goal/Objective/Service, Business Use Case, Process Flow, Event diagrams | business contract |
| **C — Information systems** | Data Entity/Data Component Catalog; Data Entity/Business Function and Application/Data matrices; Conceptual, Logical and Data Dissemination diagrams; Application Portfolio and Interface catalogs; Application/Organization, Role/Application, Application/Function, Application Interaction matrices; Application Communication, Application Use Case, Process/Application Realization, Application Migration, Software Distribution diagrams | IS contract (data + application) |
| **D — Technology** | Technology Standards and Technology Portfolio catalogs; Application/Technology and System/Technology matrices; Platform Decomposition, Processing, Environments and Locations diagrams | technology contract |
| **E — Opportunities & solutions** | gap analysis, candidate solutions, work packages; **Project Context Diagram** (the work package against the affected organisation, functions, services, applications, data and technology); **Benefits Diagram** (goals, outcomes, measurements, sub-benefits, benefits) | solution contract |
| **F — Migration planning** | roadmap, increments, dependencies, cost/benefit; the migration and delivery contracts | migration contract |
| **G — Implementation governance** | a per-delivery **compliance review** against the governing contract, its compliance level and its waivers | per-delivery compliance |
| **H — Change management** | monitoring, new requests, lessons; exactly one typed outcome — a change request with impact, or a kata candidate; a **Request for Architecture Work** when the architecture no longer meets its purpose | change review |

**Requirements management is continuous**, not a phase. The **Requirements Catalog** types every requirement as
`condition | constraint | assumption | delta`; every requirement, principle and ADR is a governed asset trace-linked
to the artefacts, contracts, cards, runs and evidence that realise it. The chain the standard defines is the trace
chain of §8.5: stakeholder and driver → goal → principle → requirement → service → evidence.

**Compliance is a typed review, not a checkbox.** A review records exactly one of the standard's relationships
between the project and the architecture specification — `irrelevant`, `consistent`, `compliant`, `conformant`,
`fully_conformant` or `non_conformant` — with its findings. A deviation is rejected, mitigated, or accepted for a
defined period through a **waiver** naming the accepting asset owner, the reason, the additional cost and risk, and
the reassessment date. A waiver without an owner and a review date is refused.

**The contracts are the gate objects.** `architecture_contract` carries four kinds across the ADM: the **Statement of
Architecture Work** (A — assignment, scope, responsibilities, acceptance criteria; distinct from the designs produced
under it), the **delivery contract** (after F — delivery commitments and the method for assessing compliance), the
**statement of intent / business usage agreement** (at completion — intended use, ownership, measures of
effectiveness), and the **Request for Architecture Work** (H — further architecture work, reviewed by the Design
Board). A contract change is a new version and re-opens its gate; the approved version's body is immutable.

**Maturity and skills are measured, not asserted.** The **architecture maturity** assessment scores nine dimensions
(architecture process; architecture development; business linkage; senior-management involvement; operating-unit
participation; architecture communication; IT security; architecture governance; IT investment and acquisition
strategy) on 0–5 (none, initial, under development, defined, managed, measured), per stage, with a baseline and
milestones. The **Architecture Skills Framework** assesses seven categories (general; business skills and methods;
architecture skills; programme/project management; general IT knowledge; technical IT skills; legal environment) at a
proficiency level per role. Both are dated rows with evidence; the development plan is a set of milestones a tranche
review can hold the capability to.

**The Architecture Board is a position set with authority rows.** It supports the architecture roadmap, assesses
proposed changes against it, applies the principles where the roadmap is incomplete, commissions solution
architectures, and submits them to the delivery Design Board. Its membership (enterprise architects, the CIO,
business-unit leaders), charter, commissioning authority and decision limits are `governance_body` rows and authority
rows, not prose.

A delivery project cannot pass its design gate without the contract that governs it; the phase-G review is per
delivery project, and its compliance level and waivers attach to that delivery's evidence. The conveyor's own
buildout runs under this capability: P0 is the Preliminary-phase and programme-definition project, and the delivery
slices T1–T17 each sit under the contract that governs them.

Scope note: this is a **tailored ADM profile** for software delivery, not a claim of TOGAF certification or full
conformance. The standard's full catalogue is the reference; the tenant's `adm_profile` names the mandatory set per
phase and plateau, and that set grows with the assessed maturity. The phases, artefacts and gates are the ones the
organisation will actually use and measure.

### 8.2 SAFe as the programme cadence

| SAFe concept | V2 implementation |
|---|---|
| Portfolio | the computed view of every project and programme in flight for the tenant; budget and strategy sit above it |
| Programme / ART | a `programme` with `shared_config`, a project dependency graph, a cadence and a standing backlog |
| PI planning | a `programme_cadence(kind='pi')` job that materialises the next cadence's draft cards from the backlog, ordered by WSJF, subject to WIP limits; a person approves the plan |
| Backlog refinement | a scheduled job that re-scores WSJF and flags stale items |
| System demo | a cadence event requiring each completed deliverable to exhibit its evidence; no demo, no credit |
| Inspect & adapt | a retro card producing lessons and kata candidates; owned by the coach |
| Lean governance | gates at value boundaries (phase/increment), not per card |

**WSJF is arithmetic, not opinion:** `(business_value + time_criticality + risk_reduction) / job_size`, all four typed
integer fields on the backlog/WBS row. The computed score is never stored; the inputs are. An LLM may draft the
narrative, never the numbers.

### 8.3 MSP as the programme definition and benefits realization

SAFe gives the programme its cadence; MSP gives it its **definition and its benefit track**. A programme is not a
large project: it is a temporary organisation that exists to deliver benefits through projects, and it is judged on
the improvement operations realizes after those projects close. V2 implements that lifecycle as rows and gates, not
as a document library.

**Capability is not use, and use is not improvement.** A delivered capability gives a team a new option. Whether the
team uses it, and whether use improves performance, are separate questions. A benefit is a **measurable improvement**
resulting from an outcome, valued by at least one stakeholder, that contributes to an organisational objective. A
`project_register_item(kind='benefit')` with no baseline, target, measurement method and owner is not a benefit; it
is a wish.

| MSP artefact | V2 row | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| Mandate — strategic fit, current position, drivers, deliverables/boundaries, delivery and assurance, success and constraints | `governed_asset(kind='mandate')` on the programme-definition project | the sponsoring group authorises the mandate |
| Programme brief — outline vision, benefit categories, cost/timescale/effort, risks and support, delivery options including doing nothing, candidate projects and timing, current operations | `governed_asset(kind='programme_brief')` | the sponsoring group approves the brief and authorises definition |
| Blueprint — processes/business models, organisation and skills, technology and data, current/intermediate/target states | `governed_asset(kind='blueprint')` + the §8.1 architecture content | blueprint contract |
| Business case — strategic objectives and realistic benefits, options including doing nothing, investment appraisal, cash flow, and how the investment delivers the capabilities the benefits depend on | `governed_asset(kind='business_case')` | investment decision; an unacceptable case returns to the future state or the project solutions |
| Benefit profile | `benefit_profile` (six field groups, below), indexed by `project_register_item(kind='benefit')` | the BCM and SRO approve; the baseline is measured before the transition |
| Benefits map | `benefit_link` edges: output → capability → operational outcome → benefit/disbenefit → strategic objective | the map is accepted with the profiles |
| Projects dossier | `project` rows + programme membership, each with outputs, resources, timescales, dependencies, requirements, budget, contribution and risks | first-tranche authorisation |
| Programme plan and tranches | `programme_tranche` + the T1 plan spine | end-of-tranche review: continue / pause / stop |
| Refined vision | `governed_asset(kind='refined_vision')` | programme board |
| Management, governance and boundary baselines | `programme_baseline(kind='management' \| 'governance' \| 'boundary')` | the baseline that the next tranche is managed against |
| Benefits management strategy and benefits realization plan | `governed_asset(kind='benefits_strategy' \| 'benefits_realization_plan')` | transition readiness |
| Stakeholder profiles | `stakeholder_profile` rows | engagement plan accepted with the profiles |
| Information, risk, issue, monitoring, communications, quality and resource strategies and plans | `governed_asset` kinds + the existing risk/issue registers (§8.4) | the programme board's governance baseline |
| Transition and realization | `benefit_transition` per benefit: baseline measured, readiness, enact, post-transition measurement, legacy retirement | the benefit review |

**The benefit profile is the measurement record.** Its six field groups are mandatory:

| Group | Fields |
|---|---|
| Identification and purpose | reference, description, category, objectives, observable outcome |
| Performance | affected KPIs, baseline, target, measurement method, financial value where expressible |
| Cost | the cost of realizing the benefit, including the associated business change |
| Conditions | capabilities required, outcomes that must already exist, changes to operating practice |
| Uncertainty and dependencies | related risks and issues, and dependencies outside the programme |
| Responsibility and attribution | who realizes it, the benefit owner (BCM), and the operational area to which the improvement is attributed |

**A tranche is not a PI.** A PI is the delivery rhythm; a tranche is the unit the programme manages and reviews
together. `programme_tranche(number, state, entry_criteria, exit_criteria, baseline_ref, review_at)` holds the unit;
the review is an approval (`gate='tranche_review'`) with the sponsoring group as approver and the baselines, the
benefit status and the risk register as its evidence. A project does not start before the first tranche is
authorised; a review continues, pauses or stops, and a re-baseline goes through change control, never through the
review itself. The preparation plan for definition is P0's own plan, not a separate artefact: it names the
resources, boundaries, controls and cost of producing the definition set.

| Tranche activity | V2 mechanism |
|---|---|
| Establish | programme board, office and working environment are positions and rows; the tranche's cards are materialised |
| Direct the work | the PM job appoints delivery, runs risk workshops, handles project exceptions and manages the teams through cards |
| Exercise control | gates, the risk/issue registers, communications, audits and assurance reviews |
| Maintain alignment | blueprint against current strategy; a deviation is a change request or a kata, never a silent fork |
| Manage resources | the resource plan, procurement and contracts as governed assets, and metering |
| Review and close | the end-of-tranche review gate, the transition to operations and the next tranche's preparation |

**Benefits realization is a procedure after delivery.** For each benefit the BCM: measures the baseline while the old
practice is still observable; monitors against the profile; plans the transition; communicates the change; assesses
readiness; enacts it; measures the post-transition performance; retires the superseded practice and system; and keeps
measuring until the realization plan names who continues after programme closure. The comparison with the baseline is
the evidence the sponsor uses to judge the change. A benefit whose baseline was never measured cannot claim an
improvement.

**Roles are positions, not code paths.** The sponsoring group, SRO, programme board, programme office, programme
manager, programme architect, BCM, PMO lead and quality manager are `job_key`s with authority rows (D50). The SRO is
accountable for the coherent capability and the benefits; the BCM owns each benefit and the transition; the PM owns
project delivery; the programme board is the SRO's decision forum. The conveyor's own buildout runs under these
roles: PM, BCM, SRO and architect are jobs using the same card, run, approval and event primitives.

**Rules.** A benefit without baseline, target, method and owner is refused. Every benefit names the capability it
depends on and the operational area that must change. A dependency slip names the benefits put at risk through the
benefit-map edges. A tranche review with no evidence is refused. A gate that never refused a tranche or a benefit in
a full cycle is flagged as broken, not healthy. The programme closes only with a realization plan that names
post-closure measurement. These rules satisfy P10: the named procedures are programme definition, tranche review and
benefits realization; the metrics are benefits realised versus planned, tranche gate outcomes and benefit-at-risk
count, all computed from rows.

### 8.4 PMP artefacts as typed rows

| PMP artefact | V2 row |
|---|---|
| Charter | `governed_asset(kind='charter')` + project |
| WBS | `wbs_node` tree |
| Scope/schedule/cost baseline | `project_baseline` (frozen snapshot, approved) |
| Risk/issue/assumption/dependency/benefit registers | `project_register_item` (one table, six kinds) |
| Change control | `project_register_item(kind='change')` + approval with impact analysis |
| Acceptance/closure | `governed_asset(kind='closure')` + DoD evidence |

The registers are deliberately one table, not five: the v4 design had separate PM tables and V1 measured RM's `pm_*`
at zero usage. One generic register with a `kind` CHECK is leaner and still queryable. The benefit profile is the one
exception: a register row indexes the benefit, and the profile holds the measurement fields that a generic register
must not carry.

### 8.5 The trace chain

```
stakeholder / driver → goal (approved)
   → principle / requirement / ADR (approved)
   → architecture artefact (approved: catalog | matrix | diagram)
   → architecture contract (approved)
   → project charter (approved)
   → WBS deliverable → work package (card) → run → step → artefact / evidence
   → acceptance (approval) → closure
```

`trace_link` is V1's existing edge; V2 requires the link at creation time for architecture-governed work. The governance
screen answers one question end to end: *which requirement does this run prove, and where is the evidence?*

### 8.6 What is not claimed

No TOGAF certification, no SAFe compliance badge, no PMP certification, no MSP certification or conformance badge. No
full ADM conformance, no ArchiMate modelling tool (a diagram is a document with typed metadata and a viewpoint, not a
live metamodel), no portfolio optimiser, no schedule solver, no benefit-forecasting model. The claim is narrower
and testable: **the artefacts and gates the organisation uses are rows, the process runs, the benefit is measured
against a baseline, and the evidence is traceable.**

## 9. Self-development and operations

### 9.1 Development projects — the conveyor builds itself

The organisation's first real job is to change its own substrate. A development project is an ordinary project with a
`development` type and a stricter gate set:

1. **Charter** names the repo, the lane, the scope and the acceptance evidence.
2. **Design note** for structural changes (architecture contract, migration plan, rollback).
3. **Lane branch** (`lane/<slug>`), one branch, at most one PR for the unit's life (house rule).
4. **Implement** through coding jobs; the executor cannot merge.
5. **Verify**: CI-equivalent locally first (fmt, clippy `-D warnings`, the full suite), then the pipeline; betterleaks;
   the relevant eval/benchmark if the change touches a measured surface.
6. **Review**: an independent reviewer job; the reviewer cannot be the implementer.
7. **Merge gate**: a human (or an earned auto-merge policy) approves; red CI is a refusal, never a retry-until-green.
8. **Deploy and verify live**: rollout by image digest, `/health`, the slice's own acceptance check; a rollback plan
   exists before the deploy.
9. **Close**: the closure record links the PR, the pipeline, the deploy evidence and the acceptance.

**Dependency repos are in scope.** A dependency change is a development project against that repo, with the same
gates; the conveyor's own dependency bump is a linked project, not a side effect. A dependency is in scope only if its
own change protocol permits an agent project; **shared infrastructure** (cluster control plane, ingress, DNS,
registry) remains a human-run change, never a development project.

### 9.2 Operations — the platform perspective

The operations job family closes the loop on the substrate:

- **Incident** is a card type with `service`, `severity`, `detected_at`, `mitigated_at`, `resolved_at` and a link to
  the run/evidence. Detection is an alert/webhook/schedule; a person can also open one.
- **Runbook** is a published procedure whose steps are k8s/git actions with gates. The first runbooks: pod crash-loop,
  rollout stuck, dependency/DB down, certificate expiry, disk pressure, queue backlog, stale lease storm.
- **Read-first**: diagnose with read actions (pods, deployments, events, logs, metrics, Flux status, git/CI). Write
  actions (restart, scale, rollback, flag flip) are `ops:write`, dry-run first, approved under the tenant's
  configured policy (default human dual control), and audited. The full write set ships in v1; autonomy is a tenant
  configuration, not a reduced feature.
- **Least privilege**: the ops connector uses a namespace-scoped service account, never cluster-admin; the action
  registry declares every verb.
- **Postmortem** is a `governed_asset`; a systemic finding becomes a kata candidate; a one-off becomes a runbook
  improvement. Blameless, evidence-linked, due within the policy window.
- **The andon cord** (V1/fr) is an incident-class action: stop new runs for a tenant/programme, keep the record, alert
  the on-call; only a person releases it.

### 9.3 Guardrails — the system cannot grade its own homework

- A development project **cannot modify the gate set, approval policy, eval instrument or benchmark suite** that
  judges it. Those are changed by a separate architecture/governance project with a different approver set.
- A kata **cannot approve** its own adoption; a kata that changed the instrument is void for that measurement.
- The **merge gate** and the **deploy gate** are separate decisions; a green CI is evidence, not an approval.
- **Auto-merge is earned**, policy-scoped and revocable: the conditions (track record, revert count, path scope,
  reviewer requirement, expiry) are tenant configuration rows, not constants in code; one revert revokes it and opens
  a kata. The default is off; the database model, the UI and the code all read the policy, never a hard-coded number.
- **Rollback is mandatory** for deployable changes; a deploy without a tested rollback is refused.
- The **benchmark harness and eval versions are frozen per measurement** (V1 D24–D26); a change to an instrument
  creates a new version and voids its sign-offs.

### 9.4 The improvement loop, end to end

```
alert / failed run / eval delta / prompt finding / coach escalation
  → coach card (one interruption, closed remedy set)
  → if systemic: kata (six Gets, evidence, candidate)
  → development project (code) or procedure/prompt/knowledge change (config)
  → measurement (benchmark / eval / run outcome, held-out)
  → adoption gate (person; dual control)
  → production (new procedure/job/binding version)
  → monitoring + lesson
```

This is one loop, not four. The kata-executor's inputs are the prompt findings and eval deltas V1 already produces;
the coach's escalations are cards; the PM's closure record is evidence; the operations postmortem feeds it back.

**The conveyor owns every decision it evaluates.** Its `decision` rows cover work routing, gates and the internal

and `procedure` rows; `release_hash` pins the immutable release. There is no imported manifest and no live copy of
another system's data.

**Channels.** The conveyor's web/Telegram/MCP channels are the **work and approval** surfaces (cards, runs, gates,
task input requests). The agent platform is a conversation front end over MCP with its own autonomy configuration; a
conversation that needs internal work opens a card across the MCP seam. Customer care is not conveyor work (D48).

the conversation, records only its own turns.

it. The family is declared here so a procedure can name the intent; the mechanism is T7's, and it is fixed to
these constraints rather than left open:

1. a **host registry** row names an addressable host and its role — a job never supplies a destination;
2. a **per-host agent** holds the host credential; the conveyor pod holds none, mirroring the broker's rule
   for tool destinations (§11.3);
3. the agent answers a **forced-command** verb set, so a compromised conveyor cannot ask for an arbitrary
   command;
4. `destructive` effect applies in full — approval, dry run and dual control (§11.4).

Until T7 lands that mechanism, `ops.host_*` operations do not exist and a procedure must not claim them.

## 11. The tool estate

**The claim.** A job is only as capable as what it may call. V2 makes the tool estate a first-class, versioned,
governed surface: every cluster service that offers a typed operation is a **tool**, tools are published in immutable
**toolkit** versions, a job's access is a **binding** with an effect ceiling, and every call is a **ledgered row**.
The conveyor owns the catalogue, the broker and the ledger. It does not route through `nonagenticai_mcp_server`
(D44), and it does not reach a backend by an ad-hoc HTTP call from a procedure or an agent.

### 11.1 Definitions — five things, one owner each

| Term | Meaning | Not to be confused with |
|---|---|---|
| **Tool** | one callable operation `<service>.<operation>`: closed input schema, output schema, effect class, idempotency, timeout, redaction, destination alias | a conveyor action (the conveyor's own op) |
| **Toolkit** | an immutable, versioned bundle of one service's tools + auth adapter + licence app + destination | a repo, a package |
| **Tool binding** | tenant-scoped grant of pinned toolkit versions to a job binding or a run, narrowed by effect ceiling, rate and credential alias | the release's tool grant |
| **Tool grant** | the release's operation allowlist (`op`, `variant`, `max_side_effect`, `enabled`) and per-call tool gate | the conveyor binding (tool existence + credential) |
| **Tool call** | one audited invocation: run/step, tool version, input hash, status, latency, bytes, cost | `action_invocation` |

**P1 applied: one owner, two rows.** The release's grant names the operations the job may use (inside the release
hash); the binding pins the toolkit versions and the credential alias. Both are conveyor rows; the release never
carries tool content, and the binding never widens the grant.

### 11.3 The broker — one call path

`tools.call` is the only way a conveyor-internal run reaches a **job backend**. The executor's own knowledge and
memory rungs are not tools: the compiled prompt's `knowledge.query` and the per-card `memory.consolidate` (§7.6) stay
where they are. A job that explicitly searches — rather than the executor grounding its prompt — uses the retrieval
toolkit like any other tool. (V1's twelve external actions — S09 Part B added eight, including
`coding_jobs.create|get`, `retrieval.query`, `artifacts.list`, `billing.summary` — are the seed of this registry and
migrate in T13: the backend operations onto toolkit operations, `artifacts.list` onto the storage adapter (§11.10).
They do not run beside it as a second path. **Settled by #450 (2026-11-19):** `artifacts.list` reads the document
catalogue, `billing.summary` reads the ledger (#46), `workers.list`/`providers.list` read the durable queue and the
host registry (§11.2), and the worker-graph catalogue read is retired with the service it described — the four
remaining are internal actions, so no External action names a non-Rust destination.)

1. **Resolve** the binding and the pinned tool version; missing binding or version fails closed (`409 tool_not_ready`)
   before any network call.
2. **Check effect** against the binding ceiling and the job authority (`403 tool_effect_forbidden`); check spend budget
   (`429 tool_budget_exceeded`).
3. **Validate** the input against the closed schema (`422 tool_input_invalid`) — `additionalProperties: false`, enums,
   patterns, bounds.
4. **Resolve the credential** from the sealed secret store by alias. The broker injects it; the prompt never carries it
   and the `tool_call` row never records it.
5. **Call the destination alias.** The base URL is registered and reviewed at publication; no caller-supplied URL at
   call time (SSRF rule). BYO destinations are tenant-allowlisted at registration.
6. **Normalise and redact**: the result envelope is `{status, data, checks[], next[]}` with
   `ok | precondition_failed | check_failed | pending | backend_error`; declared fields are redacted and the response
   size is capped.
7. **Record and emit**: one `tool_call` row (input hash, status, latency, bytes, cost) and one `tool.called` event. The
   call is never a card transition.

**Long operations are bounded.** Every poll has a fixed budget; on timeout the tool returns `pending` with a
`resume_token`, and the matching status tool continues from it. A timeout never fails silently.

**Writes verify themselves.** A write tool returns read-back `checks[]` and a `verdict`; a write with no verification
path cannot be published. Writes take an `idempotency_key`. These two rules are borrowed from the proven
`nonagenticai_mcp_server` tool contract and are not negotiable in the conveyor's registry.

### 11.4 Effect classes and gates

| Class | Examples | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| **read** | scrape, search, retrieve, pod status, CI status | none; audit only |
| **write** | code write, test run, PR, artifact upload, report assembly | job authority + audit; no human gate by default |
| **destructive** | k8s restart/scale/rollback, branch delete, data purge | approval + dry-run + dual control (`ops:write`) |
| **spend** | LLM generation, w2v render, TTS, paid data source | budget check + ledger |

A binding's ceiling narrows only: a job may lower its effect class at run time, never raise it. The mapping is data on
the tool version; it is not inferred from the HTTP method.

**Tool selection is not an LLM decision.** In a procedure run the step names its tool; a step that must choose among
tools uses L1 over the bound option set. In an `internal_agent` run the release's grant set bounds what the agent may
choose, and every choice is recorded; the broker never widens the grant.

### 11.5 BYO tools (D42)

A tenant may bring two kinds of tool and only two:

1. **OpenAPI toolkit** — an OpenAPI 3.1 document imported as a draft toolkit: operations, closed schemas, mappings,
   effect class per operation (default `read`), a destination base URL and a credential alias. Publication needs
   tenant-admin approval and a contract test against a recorded replay.
2. **Remote MCP server** — a streamable-HTTP MCP endpoint; the conveyor discovers its tools, binds a credential and
   exposes only the bound subset to the tenant's jobs (binding-scoped discovery).

Never: uploaded code, arbitrary container images, caller-supplied URLs at call time, or a tenant credential in a
prompt. The conveyor never executes tenant code; a tenant that needs executable logic runs its own service and
registers it. A tenant toolkit stays tenant-scoped; promoting it to the platform catalogue is a kata/development
project with a platform review, never an admin toggle.

### 11.6 Tools that generate tools (D43)

Development projects already act through the coding toolkit. Three generation paths, all governed:

1. **Spec → toolkit.** An OpenAPI document (a new service, or one being changed) is imported as draft operations,
   contract-tested, then published.
2. **Service → toolkit.** A new service is scaffolded from `template-rust-service`, deployed, and its OpenAPI is
   registered — the tool is the new service, not a wrapper around it.
3. **Missing operation → tool request.** A procedure step that needs an operation with no tool opens a tool-request
   card; a development job implements it, publishes the version, and the step is rebound to that pin.

The pipeline is a governed-asset lifecycle: `governed_asset(kind='tool_draft')` → validation (schema, effect, egress,
credential scope) → security review (a destructive tool needs a named approver) → `tools.publish` (immutable version)
→ binding. A tool cannot be published with wildcard egress, a free-form input schema, or a write effect without an
idempotency declaration. The tool that publishes a tool is itself a tool bound to the authoring job — and cannot
grant itself a wider effect ceiling.

**Tool code lives in the conveyor monorepo (D58).** A new tool is a crate or service inside the conveyor workspace,
registered from its own OpenAPI; a migrated tool joins the workspace on the day it is rewritten in Rust. An external
service stays bindable as a toolkit meanwhile. Nothing is imported from `nonagenticai_mcp_server`'s `toolkits/`
(`coding`, `fr`) — those are read as reference only (D44).

### 11.7 Relationship to `nonagenticai_mcp_server` (D44)

**Concepts borrowed (measured 2026-11-11):** the catalog shape — `mcp_services`/`mcp_sources` →
`mcp_tool_versions`/`mcp_toolkit_versions` → `mcp_bindings` with `mcp_credential_profiles` →
`mcp_tool_call_audit`; immutable version pinning; the closed Draft 2020-12 schema subset; binding-scoped MCP
discovery; the credential broker; the result envelope; write-verify. The server ships two toolkits today — `coding`
(11 operations) and `fr` (3) — and its `mcp_tool_call_audit` is the direct model for `tool_call`. **Not adopted:**
ephemeral Kata execution — BYO is declarative only, so the conveyor never runs uploaded code.

**Dependency refused.** The mcp server is a second control plane: Python, its own Postgres queue, its own catalog and
runner. The conveyor already owns actions, secrets, entitlements, audit and a durable job queue. One repo, one
schema, one queue (owner direction, 2026-11-11). The mcp server remains the **agent platform's** gateway for its own
backends; it is that platform's own roadmap, and the conveyor never routes through it. Its `coding` toolkit (repo
provisioning, verified writes, PRs) is the reference for the conveyor's coding toolkit. The `fr` toolkit retires with
fr at cutover (V1 D19).

**Two paths, permanently (D59).** There is no planned convergence: the agent platform keeps its own gateway, and the
conveyor broker is not exposed to it. "One audit path" is explicitly not a V2 goal; the conveyor's ledger covers
conveyor jobs only (§15.2 #11).

### 11.8 Data model and actions

| Table | Purpose | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `tool` | one operation version | input/output schema, effect, idempotency, timeout, redact, destination alias, status |
| `toolkit` | a service's published bundle | immutable `key@version`, auth adapter, licence app, owner |
| `tool_binding` | job/run access | tenant-scoped, pinned toolkit versions, effect ceiling, credential alias, enabled |
| `tool_call` | the call ledger | run/step, tool version, input hash, status, latency, bytes, cost |

Reused, not created: V1 `secret` (credential storage), `governed_asset(kind='tool_draft')`, `event`, `audit_event`,
`inference_call` (for a spend tool that causes model calls). A tool call is **not** an `action_invocation` and never
transitions a card. The actions are the `tools.*` family in §10.4; each is an `ActionSpec` like every other action, so
it is served over HTTP, MCP and OpenAPI from one declaration.

### 11.9 Metrics, health and retirement

Per tool: calls, success rate, p95 latency, error classes, cost. Per job: tool-budget usage. Every published tool has
a `tools.probe` (read-only health); a probe failure unbinds the tool from new runs (`409 tool_not_ready`) while
in-flight runs finish. A tool with zero calls over one programme cycle is flagged and retired (P10). A schema-drift
signature — the backend changed under the contract — opens a kata, not a silent retry.

### 11.10 Object storage — direct MinIO, tenant-separated (D57)

The conveyor does not depend on `artifact_service` :8556 or `storage-api` :8391 for its own bytes. One storage adapter
writes and reads the platform's shared MinIO instance directly — not a private store — with tenant separation
enforced by key prefix and bucket policy: a mandatory tenant prefix (`tenant/<tenant_id>/`), project/run prefixes
beneath it, server-side encryption, a content hash per object, a size cap, and no bucket administration from a job. Credentials
are sealed broker credential profiles; a job never sees an S3 key. `artifact_service` and `storage-api` keep serving
their existing consumers; the conveyor keeps no compatibility shim — `artifacts.list` was migrated onto this
catalogue's own store by #450 (§15.2 #17).

| R1 | **Over-abstraction** — the v4 lesson: four `wf_*` types "serve nothing", the generator was deleted | P10: no aggregate without a named procedure and a metric; T0–T3 only the spine; kill any table with zero use after one programme cycle |

| R9 | **Scale of the catalogue** — thousands of jobs become unmanageable | derivation + curation; department/job search; publish in waves; metrics per job; retire by evidence |

| R11 | **MCP contract break at cutover** | V1 R11 stands: the tool surface is versioned; S06b's tool-contract test; a job release pins the expected tool keys |
| R12 | **Operations blast radius** | read-first; namespace-scoped service account; dry-run; dual control; andon; no cluster-admin |
| R13 | **Tool sprawl** — dozens of unowned backends; a tool nobody calls | one toolkit owner per service; `tools.probe`; zero-use retirement after a programme cycle (P10); bindings reviewed with the job |

8. ~~Legacy kag.~~ **Resolved direction (D54):** a Rust rewrite; the home of each capability — including neo4j,

9. ~~External source migration.~~ **Resolved direction (D54):** migrate or rewrite into the conveyor's estate;
   re-architecture is allowed where a line-port would not fit; external sources stay behind services until then.
10. ~~mcp_server migration.~~ **Closed:** the mcp server is the agent platform's own gateway; it is outside the

12. ~~n8n legacy visibility.~~ **Closed:** n8n is reference only — a previous design that is superseded. No
    operations job reads its execution history; it is not a tool.
13. ~~Procedure ontology depth.~~ **Resolved direction (D53, amended 2026-11-19):** procedural knowledge is the
    published procedure itself; the action space is its PDDL steps, and RDF/OWL ingestion produces a strata
    knowledge pack the procedure pins (`knowledge_pack_ref`) — there is no relational ontology store. How deep the

    project may override is tenant policy. *Open.*
17. **`artifact_service` compatibility.** D57 removes the dependency; whether V1's `artifacts.list` callers move to
    the MinIO adapter inside T13, or a temporary shim is kept, is a T13 implementation decision.
    **Resolved (#450, 2026-11-19):** `artifacts.list` reads the conveyor's own document/object catalogue; no shim.
18. **`mlx-api` consolidation.** `modality-gateway` folds into `mlx-api`, which may be rewritten in Rust; the owning
    repo, the rewrite order and how the w2v stages call it are decided with the w2v migration (`SPEC_LEGACY_KAG.md`).
    *Open.*
19. ~~AHTAPol and w2v tenant shape.~~ **Resolved (D60):** AHTAPol is its own tenant with industry

    runtime is deferred until D61's four conditions hold. The product boundary stays `/mcp`; only stateless
    infrastructure is shared (inference-router, strata, MinIO, tool backends). *Open until D61 is accepted; if
    rejected, decide the split here.*

---

## Appendix A — Vocabulary

| Term | Meaning | Not to be confused with |
|---|---|---|
| **Industry / department / job** | the organisational placement of a position | a tenant, a project, a card |
| **Job** | a configured position with a charter, capability binding, procedure, inference config and authority | `capability` (an ability), `capability_agent` (a conveyor-local executor config) |
| **Capability** | what the organisation can do (design, build, test, govern, operate) | a job (who does it) |
| **Procedure** | executable documentation: ordered steps, each an action + optional gate | a job (the position), a run (one attempt) |
| **Card** | the work package; the unit of assignment | a run (one execution), a conversation turn |
| **Run** | one attempt at a card through an executor | a job (the position), a card (the assignment) |
| **Executor** | the mechanism that executes a run: `procedure` or `internal_agent` behind one contract | a job (the position), a runtime backend |
| **Approval** | a decision/gate; a question is an approval | a comment, a notification |
| **Binding** | the join of a job to its immutable release, capability, procedure and executor | the release row itself |
| **Portfolio** | every project and programme in flight for a tenant — a computed view, never a row | a programme (a set of projects with shared config) |
| **Programme** | a set of projects with shared configuration and project-level dependencies; carries budget and cadence | a project (a temporary endeavour), the portfolio (a computed view) |
| **Kata** | a system-improvement job using the six Gets | a bug fix, a retry |
| **Coach** | the flow-protection job; triage + bounded remedies | a PM (plan and scope) |
| **Laya** | the System-1 calibrated choice/score/noul model | an LLM (generation) |
| **Tool** | one typed callable operation on a backend (`<service>.<operation>`) | a conveyor action, a capability |
| **Toolkit** | an immutable, versioned bundle of one service's tools | a package, a repo |
| **Tool binding** | tenant-scoped access to pinned toolkit versions with an effect ceiling | a tool grant (the release's op allowlist) |
| **Tool call** | one audited invocation through the broker | an `action_invocation` |
| **Storage adapter** | the conveyor's own MinIO client with tenant-separated prefixes and sealed credentials | `artifact_service`, `storage-api`, an S3 key in a prompt |
| **Effect class** | read / write / destructive / spend — the gate a call must pass | a role scope |
| **PDDL** | Planning Domain Definition Language — the notation a procedure step is written in | a prompt, a task description |
| **Action space** | the PDDL step: an action with preconditions and effects over typed facts, inside a procedure | a packed domain knowledge set (the procedure names its pack) |
| **Procedural knowledge** | the published procedure itself — intent, ordered steps, actions, gates, declared outputs and failure branches — versioned and pinned by a run | a separate ontology store (removed by the owner decision of 2026-11-19) |
| **Decision policy refinement** | a tenant's versioned override of a platform decision case (threshold/rule, fail action, laya config) | the platform `decision_policy` itself |
| **Authoring** | the job family that drafts tenant assets from chat input and documents | a chat assistant (it drafts; it never publishes) |
| **SOP** | a standard operating procedure a tenant supplies (PDF, URL, document) and the conveyor converts | the procedure itself, a prompt |
| **Continuous line** | standing, repeatable work (operations) as opposed to a temporary project | a project (a temporary endeavour) |

## Appendix B — V1 decisions: retained, amended, superseded

| V1 decision | V2 status |
|---|---|
| D1–D5, D7–D17 (build location, parity, scope, UI, data, cutover, procedures, API, identity, channels) | **Retained** |
| D6 (n8n later — in-app engine + `egui_xyflow` editor) | **Retained in V1, clarified by V2**: V1 S13 owns the in-app engine and the internal agent loop (`agent.run`) and re-authors the flows as procedures; V2 uses that engine as its procedure executor. The n8n product itself is reference only — a superseded design, not a tool (owner, 2026-11-11) |
| D18 (agent interface via `mcp_server`) | **Already superseded by V1's own D19** (2026-11-08); the surviving rule — a question is an approval — is carried into §6.6 |
| D19 (agent calls the conveyor's `/mcp`) | **Retained**; the agent platform is a user-interaction front end over MCP (D33) |
| D20 (capability/knowledge/memory) | **Extended** by D28 (organisation layer), D33 (ownership), D36 (lessons), D37 (metrics). One clarification: the conveyor owns the job release and its knowledge pins; there is no second copy in the agent platform |
| D21 (MCP tasks) / D22 (executor model) | **D21 retained. D22 amended by D46; D61 (proposed) adds the seam**: two live executor kinds (`procedure`, `internal_agent`) behind one internal `Executor` contract, with an extensible kind once D61 is accepted; the external agent executor is retired; an external runtime is a non-goal until D61's conditions hold; the conveyor never depends on `agent` |
| D23 (inference ledger/prompt audit) | **Retained**; D30 adds the decision ledger beside it |
| D24–D27 (benchmark, eval, hillclimb, compiled prompts) | **Retained**; they are the instruments D32/D37/P5 rely on. D27 governs every prompt the conveyor runs, including the internal agent's (§7.7) |
| D19's statement that `nonagenticai_mcp_server` remains the agent platform's gateway for every other backend | **Retained for the agent platform; amended for the conveyor** by D44: the conveyor implements its own broker and never routes through it |
| D14 (adjacent services — `artifacts` not absorbed) | **Amended by D57**: `artifact_service`/`storage-api` stay outside, but the conveyor does not call them for its own bytes — it uses MinIO directly under tenant prefixes |
| No V1 decision is superseded **by V2** | D18 was superseded by V1's own D19; D6 is clarified (V1's in-app engine is the executor; the n8n product is reference only); D14 is amended by D57; V2 adds D28–D61 and does not re-open the V1 build |

## Appendix C — What we carry from the old design, and what we delete

**Carried (concepts):** PM owns the project structure and is the only project writer after the request; per-phase and
per-artefact sign-offs; WIP limits on ready/doing; one coach card per interruption; the closed remedy set; the six
Gets; unique open kata signature; a failed kata keeps the andon cord until a person releases it; "no data, no
improvement"; measure live callers before deleting anything. One deliberate change: the old kata could not touch
**procedures** (measured 0 of 334 active flows); V2's procedures are first-class and kata may change them — the old
exclusion was a measurement of zero use, not a principle.

**Deleted (mechanism):** Planka as the state owner; 280 generated card-type × list flows; the flow generator; four
`wf_*` types; the open-ended coach LLM rung; kata pausing the whole conveyor for 30–45 minutes; duplicate card birth
(non-idempotent plumbing); 35 uncovered error exits; the Python substrate.

**Measured evidence:** E32 duplicate card birth; 35 uncovered error exits E1–E35; the kata record showed no kata
closed (the source records a moving count — 9, then 10, then 11 the same day — and warns against quoting it); the
generator deleted because "the live flow is the truth" (`n8n-designs/design/choices/v4`, `kata_v1.html`).

---

*End of SPEC V2. The V1 build record remains `docs/SPEC.md`; the slice plans remain `docs/plans/`. On approval, this
file is registered in `~/.claude/plans/program/INDEX.md`, the ownership matrix is signed, and T0 opens.*

# Closure — SPEC-V2, retrospective (2026-11-21)

**Retrospective closure.** The project was first closed on 2026-11-17 without a closure review and without declared closure outputs. This record closes the reworked project through the one gate; it is written 2026-11-21 under the standing delegation `01a1ff1f-e4ba-72dc-9c1a-13049933cf14` and claims no 2026-11-17 act it cannot show.

## What was delivered

`docs/SPEC_V2.md` — **SPEC V2, conveyor: the organisational operating model** (dated 2026-11-11, amended 2026-11-19; 1,793 lines; decisions D28–D63). The spec's thesis: an organisation is a set of positions making decisions and doing work under governance; there are four units only — job, card, approval, run — and everything else is a view or an instrument. It defines the organisation spine (industry → department(s) → job, immutable releases, tenant-scoped bindings), the work hierarchy (portfolio computed, programme with shared_config and a project dependency graph, project, WBS, card, run), the decision ladder (rule → laya → generation → human), the meta-jobs, TOGAF/SAFe/PMP/MSP as executable rows and gates, the tool estate (catalogue, broker, ledger) and self-development and operations under the same gates.

## Closure outputs

- `evidence` — the manifest's verified result and the acceptance evidence.
- `closure-review` — the published review whose four sections are Outcome vs acceptance, Evidence, Open items and Decision.

## Acceptance

`acceptance/programme/SPEC-V2.toml` — *the closure review exists and every declared closure output is published; the project re-closes through the one gate.* Every check is P0: project closed, approved baseline, approved charter, closure outputs, live board-approved delivery contract, a Phase-G review citing the published delegation, a closure gate decided by a distinct approver, no expired or self-owned waiver, PI and refinement cadence rows, WSJF inputs on the WBS deliverable, and a demo credit for the accepted deliverable. The project closes only on a green verdict; the closure gate records that verdict as its evidence.

## Benefit

B1 — **Auditable decisions**: target as recorded, *every choice has a decision row*; measured by counting decision rows per run from the action ledger; serving objective O3. The baseline as recorded is `not measured - no instrument exists (recorded as a kata on the kata project)`, and the profile's operational area is empty in the record. No improvement is claimed.

## Not recoverable

- Who closed the project on 2026-11-17, and on what rationale: no approval row and no closure asset exists.
- The contemporaneous WSJF inputs: none were scored before 2026-11-21.
- B1's baseline value: no instrument measured it.
- A contemporaneous Statement of Architecture Work and compliance review: neither was recorded.

## Residual open items

§15.2 questions #6, #14, #15, #16, #18, #20 and #21 remain open, and D61 remains proposed. None is a V2 premise: the spec names them as decisions for T1, T16, T17 and `docs/SPEC_LEGACY_KAG.md`.

# Benefits Diagram — SPEC-V2 (retrospective, 2026-11-26)

## Goals and outcomes

The goal is an organisation the conveyor owns and can prove: positions that are catalogued, released and bound; work that moves from programme to run with a baseline, a register and evidence; and decisions that pass rule → laya → generation → human with every step recorded. The measurable outcome is auditability at the level of a single decision — which option, which confidence, which policy, which person, which evidence (§13). The plan calls this the unglamorous win, and it is the outcome the benefit depends on.

## Measures

The measures are computed read models, never stored opinions (D37): flow (lead time, cycle time, queue time, block time, flow efficiency, WIP, throughput), quality (first-pass yield, rework rate, defect escapes, eval score, benchmark delta), cost from the ledger, governance (gate latency, approval rate, override rate, evidence completeness, never-refused gates) and knowledge (pack hit rate, citation rate, readiness blocks, lesson promotion). Metering rolls up at tenant, department, programme, project and job and drills to run, step and call, reconciled with billing_service (D52). A gate that never refused in a full cycle is flagged as broken.

## Benefits and sub-benefits

The benefit is auditability at the level of a single decision. Its sub-benefits are a staffed improvement loop — coach, kata, development, measurement and adoption as one loop (§9.4); a programme cadence in which a PI is the delivery rhythm and a tranche is the managed unit, with the review an approval carrying baselines, benefit status and the risk register (§8.2, §8.3); and executable rigour, with TOGAF, SAFe, PMP and MSP as rows and gates and no certification claim (§8.6). A benefit without baseline, target, method and owner is refused, so no sub-benefit can be claimed on a wish.

# Candidate Solutions — SPEC-V2 (retrospective, 2026-11-26)

## Candidates

Four routes were considered. The first keeps V1 and adds ad-hoc agents, which preserves the working machine and leaves the organisation, cadence and meta-jobs absent. The second adopts a field framework — CrewAI, ChatDev/DevAll or n8n — and inherits their conversation model. The third is V2 as specified: the conveyor owns the whole model in four units, with typed rows and gates. The fourth adds an external executor runtime beside the internal one, and D61 defers it until four stated conditions hold.

## Criteria

The routes are judged on five criteria the plan already fixes: one record per fact (P1), so no concept is stored twice; no speculative aggregate (P10), so a table exists only because a named procedure uses it and a metric reads it; tenant configuration over code (P11), so policies are versioned rows; self-containment (D33), so the conveyor owns its model and the agent platform is a front end; and measurement before adoption (P5), so a change is adopted because a held-out instrument moved. A sixth, narrower criterion is honesty of claim: no certification or conformance badge (§8.6).

## Options rejected

Keeping V1 and adding ad-hoc agents is rejected because the organisation spine, the programme cadence, the meta-jobs and the operations perspective do not exist, and the improvement loop has nothing staffing it. The field frameworks are rejected because they build agent conversations, while organisations run on positions, work products, gates, baselines and evidence; the measured n8n estate — 348 workflows, 280 of them the generated card-type by list matrix, each with its own error exits — is the plan's own caution (§1.3, §1.4). The external runtime is deferred, not rejected: D61 names the four conditions, and the seam in T0 preserves the option at near-zero cost.

# Project Context Diagram — SPEC-V2 (retrospective, 2026-11-26)

## Context

The work package is the SPEC-V2 definition set: the plan `docs/SPEC_V2.md`, its decisions and the architecture artefacts it governs. Its boundary is the model the conveyor owns — organisation, work, decisions, programme cadence, architecture, tools and measurement — together with the rows, contracts and gates that make each one executable. The context is the first tenant `nonagentic`, industry `software`, with AHTAPol and w2v as separate tenants and industries (D60), and with the delivery slices T0 to T19F as the work that carries the model into the estate.

## Affected organisation

The programme owner and sponsor decides and chairs the Architecture Board; the programme architect authors under the #526 delegation; the Board approves contracts and artefacts. The first departments are delivery, verification, operations, project office and improvement, and their jobs are the first positions the model must staff — conveyor maintenance first, then feature delivery, then operations (§4.6). Development projects act as the system's own capacity to change its substrate, and the agent platform is a front end whose users reach the same work over MCP. Independent reviewers and the public read the published design.

## Affected systems

The conveyor application is one binary on port 8930 with no new port (V2 adds tables and actions), live on 3 pods with `/health` and `/health/ready` 200 on the 2026-11-10 deploy record. laya answers on :9210 behind a Jev-compatible bridge. strata_ingest and strata_rag hold knowledge packs and one cold digest per card. MinIO holds bytes directly under tenant prefixes, with no artifact_service or storage-api dependency. The agent platform reaches the conveyor over `/mcp`; billing_service remains the charging system the metering reconciles to.

# Spec — SPEC-V2 (retrospective, 2026-11-26)

## Context

V1 built one Rust application that carries work: projects, boards, lists, cards, runs, approvals, procedures, capabilities, capability agents, knowledge and memory bindings, an inference ledger, a native SWE-bench harness, evals and the compiled-prompt pipeline. Its last whole-tree checkpoint of 2026-11-09 measured 83 tables and 243 actions as a floor, and the app is live at `conveyor.nonagentic.ai` on main `85487a04`, 3 pods, with `/health` and `/health/ready` 200 on `:8930` (deploy record 2026-11-10). V1 answers how work is carried; it does not answer who the organisation is. Three independently built things — the `agent` platform as a user of the conveyor over MCP, the KH hierarchy proving positions, departments and immutable releases, and the conveyor's own work and proof rows — have arrived at the same shape, and the missing piece is the organisation. The field builds agent conversations; real organisations run on positions, work products, gates, baselines and evidence.

## Requirements

The requirements are the plan's hard invariants and its binding decisions. One record per fact: no concept is stored in two systems, and systems join by pinned reference. No work without a card; no transition without an action; no completion without evidence. The executor never approves its own work, and dual control is two or more distinct approvers. Rule → laya → generation → human: an LLM never selects, routes, classifies or approves, and a generated output is a draft with no path to a state transition. Every model call is ledgered and budgeted; an unresolved binding, pack, prompt source or tool fails closed with `409 *_not_ready` before the first call. No speculative aggregate: a table exists because a named procedure uses it and a metric reads it. Tenant configuration over code: every policy, threshold, limit and approval kind is a versioned tenant-scoped row with a platform default. Requirements are typed condition, constraint, assumption or delta and are managed continuously, not by phase.

## Design

The design has four units and nothing else: a job (a position — a capability, a procedure, an inference configuration and an authority), a card (a work package), an approval (the one human-escalation primitive, where a question is an approval) and a run (one recorded attempt). Departments, programmes and portfolios organise them; knowledge, memory and tools configure them; evals, benchmarks and the ledger measure them; a meeting is a decision forum over them. The organisation spine is industry → department(s), ordered → job, with knowledge layered base → industry → department archetype → each department in order → job, compiled into an immutable release; a binding pins `job_key`, `release_hash` and a `release_snapshot`, and a retired binding refuses `409 job_binding_stale` before any model call. The work hierarchy is tenant → portfolio (computed, never a row) / programme (shared_config plus project dependency edges) → project → WBS → card → run → step. TOGAF ADM, SAFe, PMP and MSP are rows and gates: phases are WBS nodes, artefacts are typed rows with entries and links, gates are approvals, tranches are the programme's management unit, and a benefit without baseline, target, method and owner is refused. The tool estate is a catalogue of immutable toolkit versions, a binding with an effect ceiling and one `tool_call` row per call, all through one in-process broker; bytes go directly to MinIO under tenant prefixes.

## Acceptance

The acceptance is executable. `python3 scripts/verify-project.py --project SPEC-V2 --snapshot <fresh>` is green with 11 checks and 0 failures at `d7293f96`, the strict audit on the same snapshot carries no P0/P1 entry, and the acceptance manifest `acceptance/programme/SPEC-V2.toml` is the gate's evidence. The seven A–D artefacts are approved rows published 2026-11-22 and the eight E–H artefacts are authored on 2026-11-26; the Phase-G review records level compliant; the project re-closes through the one gate with an approver other than its requester. The plan's own slice acceptance is narrower and testable: T0 proves that a job is created, a release published, a binding pinned and a run on a retired binding refused; later slices each carry a named refusal. No TOGAF certification, SAFe compliance badge, PMP certification, MSP conformance or full ADM conformance is claimed, and that restraint is part of the acceptance.
